research_question: What does the primary literature support as practical acceptance logic for LLM-generated economic-research labels, while distinguishing production labeling from downstream inferential acceptance?

bottom_line.universal_threshold: None of the reviewed papers supplies a universal accuracy, F1, agreement, or correlation cutoff at which LLM labels become acceptable. Grimmer and Stewart explicitly make validation problem-specific and show that researchers decide whether observed performance is sufficient for the application.
bottom_line.researcher_decision: Acceptance must be tied to the research construct, target population, error costs, and downstream quantity of interest. Numeric gates therefore require a documented project decision; they should not be presented as literature-mandated constants.
bottom_line.agreement_is_not_accuracy: Repeated-model or AI-AI agreement is evidence of stability only. Gilardi et al. define accuracy and intercoder agreement as different metrics, while Asirvatham et al. distinguish agreement with human judgments from external/ground-truth validity. Two systems can agree and still be wrong in the same way.
bottom_line.generation_vs_inference: A stable pipeline may be ready to generate provisional production labels before those labels are acceptable as plug-in measurements for causal or descriptive inference. Ludwig et al. require validation data to assess and correct measurement error for downstream estimation; absent reliable reference labels, AI-only agreement cannot supply that guarantee.
bottom_line.no_human_review_no_api_constraint: Because this project declines human review and currently has no API, the reviewed human-benchmark and API-scale results cannot be treated as project validation or proof of deployable throughput. They support a design for later validation, not a claim that current labels are human-validated. Prediction-powered or debiasing methods also cannot repair inference without reliable validation measurements.

practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.supported_standard: Define each construct and label rule before scaling; freeze the operational codebook/prompt version and record any examples, model, generation settings, and post-processing. Treat a changed prompt or model as a changed measurement procedure that must be re-evaluated.
practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.status: literature-supported workflow principle; no universal numeric gate
basis: Grimmer and Stewart: research questions and quantities of interest imply different models and validation methods.
Ludwig, Mullainathan, and Rambachan: seemingly innocuous prompt/model choices can change downstream estimates.
Gilardi et al.: all annotator groups received the same task instructions, making the codebook part of the evaluated procedure.

practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.supported_standard: Use a held-out or otherwise out-of-sample evaluation design for the exact target population and report field/class-specific confusion information rather than relying on one aggregate agreement score. Stratification by field, class prevalence, source, time, or other consequential slices is a defensible project design when those slices may have different error patterns.
practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.status: held-out evaluation is direct guidance; the particular stratification variables and thresholds are researcher decisions
basis: Grimmer and Stewart: separate training, validation, and test roles; cross-validation keeps predictions out of sample; confusion matrices reveal class-specific precision and recall hidden by overall accuracy.
Ludwig, Mullainathan, and Rambachan: researchers must define the target population and sampling procedure for evaluation.
Asirvatham, Mokski, and Shleifer: broad evaluation spans many topics and task types, so broad claims rest on cross-domain testing rather than a single aggregate example.

practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.supported_standard: Production can be staged when the frozen procedure is operationally stable and its observed failure profile is documented, with labels explicitly treated as provisional measurements. Escalate or quarantine fields/slices whose errors are unknown or material to the intended use. The literature supports application-specific sufficiency rather than perfection, but it does not authorize a particular pass number.
practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.status: synthesis from the sources; project owners must choose loss-based gates
basis: Grimmer and Stewart present a 0.65-accuracy example and state that scholars may judge it sufficient depending on the application or take steps to improve it; this is an illustration of decision dependence, not a recommended threshold.
Asirvatham, Mokski, and Shleifer explicitly say their goal is not to claim flawless measurement and test multiple threats to validity.

practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.supported_standard: Before using labels as measured outcomes or covariates in economic estimation, quantify remaining misclassification/measurement error against reliable validation measurements and propagate or sensitivity-test its effect on the reported estimand. Label-generation readiness alone does not satisfy this inference gate.
practical_acceptance_logic_supported_by_.status: direct econometric requirement in Ludwig et al.; implementation requires reliable validation data
basis: Ludwig, Mullainathan, and Rambachan: absent validation data, the magnitude and pattern of LLM errors and their effect on downstream parameters cannot be assessed; a small validation sample can be used for bias correction and valid inference.
Grimmer and Stewart: uncertainty in text-derived measurements should be carried into downstream models.

sources.citation: Justin Grimmer and Brandon M. Stewart (2013), Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts, Political Analysis 21(3):267-297.

claims.claim: Automated text methods require extensive, problem-specific validation; performance on a new dataset is not guaranteed.
There is no globally best method: the research question and quantity of interest determine useful models and validation methods.
For supervised classification, an ideal workflow separates training, validation, and test roles; V-fold cross-validation approximates this while keeping evaluated predictions out of sample.

Overall accuracy can conceal category-specific behavior; confusion matrices, precision, and recall diagnose the error profile. Whether demonstrated performance is sufficient depends on the application.
A reported 0.65 accuracy in the worked example is not a recommended gate; the authors use it to show that sufficiency is application-dependent.

sources.citation: Jens Ludwig, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Ashesh Rambachan, Large Language Models: An Applied Econometric Framework, NBER Working Paper 33344; arXiv revision v4 dated December 5, 2025, later Annual Review of Economics 2026.

claims.claim: The paper separates prediction from estimation. Prediction evaluation requires no training leakage; estimation using LLM labels as measurements requires validation data for valid downstream inference.
claims.locator: Abstract; Section 1; Sections 3 and 4; Section 6 checklist

claims.claim: For evaluation, researchers must define the target population and sampling procedure; an evaluation sample reflects out-of-sample performance only under the required no-leakage condition.

In estimation, prompt/model choices can yield materially different coefficients, signs, and significance. Without a validation sample, researchers cannot assess the magnitude or pattern of errors or their downstream effect.
claims.locator: Section 1, especially the discussion corresponding to HTML lines 109-115; Sections 4.2 and 4.4

claims.claim: A small validation sample can support empirical bias correction and consistent/asymptotically normal inference, but the method presupposes a reliable target measurement procedure in that validation sample.
For this project, AI-AI agreement without reliable validation labels does not meet the paper's estimation safeguard and cannot by itself justify plug-in inferential use.

sources.citation: Hemanth Asirvatham, Elliott Mokski, and Andrei Shleifer (2026), GPT as a Measurement Tool, NBER Working Paper 34834.

claims.claim: Measurement validity is assessed through distinct threats: agreement with human judgments, external validity against ground truth, prompt brittleness/noise, and whether measurement is direct rather than driven by contamination or shortcuts.
claims.locator: Section 4.1, threats to validity, approximately pp. 17-19

claims.claim: Human labels are not necessarily ground truth. Agreement with humans is a first-pass validation, while external outcomes can test whether a measure captures real signal.

The authors evaluate more than 1,000 classification tasks across more than 300 text datasets and examine performance across topic/task types; this supports their broad empirical claim but does not create a universal acceptance threshold for a new project.
Semantically equivalent prompt formulations should yield stable measurements, while substantively different attribute definitions should change results where relevant.
claims.locator: Section 4.1, item 3, prompt brittleness and noise

claims.claim: The authors explicitly do not claim flawless LLM measurement; their API-based GABRIEL evidence is not a substitute for validating this project's no-human-review, no-API workflow.
claims.locator: Opening of Section 4 and GABRIEL implementation description

sources.citation: Fabrizio Gilardi, Meysam Alizadeh, and Mael Kubli (2023), ChatGPT Outperforms Crowd-Workers for Text-Annotation Tasks, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 120(30):e2305016120.

claims.claim: Accuracy and intercoder agreement are separate metrics: accuracy is correctness against an agreed trained-human reference, while intercoder agreement measures whether two annotators in a group return the same class.

The study's accuracy calculations use trained-human annotations as a gold standard only on items where both trained annotators agreed. Therefore its evidence does not justify treating model-model agreement alone as accuracy.
claims.locator: Materials and Methods, Trained Annotators and Evaluation Metrics

claims.claim: The exact same annotation instructions were given to ChatGPT, trained annotators, and crowd workers. This makes the task definition/codebook an integral part of the evaluated labeling procedure.
claims.locator: Materials and Methods, Annotation Tasks, Trained Annotators, Crowd Workers, and ChatGPT

claims.claim: The study used the gpt-3.5-turbo API and repeated calls. Its cost and scale findings do not establish feasibility for a project with no API.

sources.citation: Anne Lundgaard Hansen (2026), Validating Large Language Model Annotations, FEDS 2026-020, March 11 draft.

claims.claim: Proposes annotation backtranslation, separation, and reconstruction tests when reliable external benchmark labels are unavailable.
Opposing systematic errors can evade the framework; results depend on simulation prompts and semantic embeddings.

This is a recent working-paper proposal, not a universal professional acceptance standard. We do not reproduce its tests; exact evidence checking and boundary cases do not establish that its prerequisites passed.

non_claims: No reviewed source mandates a universal 80%, 90%, 0.8 kappa, or other numeric acceptance threshold.
AI-AI agreement is not evidence of truth unless connected to an independently credible reference or external outcome.
Few-shot examples or a detailed codebook do not eliminate the need to evaluate the final frozen procedure; they are components of that procedure.
Production generation of labels does not by itself authorize their use as error-free regressors, outcomes, treatments, or controls.
Prediction-powered inference, debiasing, or measurement-error correction cannot identify and fix bias without reliable validation measurements.
Results from API-based studies do not solve the current project's lack of an API or create a validated human benchmark when human review is refused.
